messages.author: 70f4b2a8c58d14bd
messages.subject: long autorcorrelations
parts:
hi

thx u all for developing this Stan, it is really great to have such a well documented and solid work available...

I recently installed Stan on my machine (osx 10.9) to give it a try in an attempt to replicate my previous results from jags.

To make few tests, I created  29 x and y pairs with minimal noise, the intercept and slope parameters are as follows:
[ones(length(x),1) x-mean(x)]\y

ans =

    0.6231
    4.0016

 
I set to run the following model, adapted from the rats.stan (I subtract the mean of x before feeding it in stan)


model {
  mu_alpha ~ normal(0, 100);
  mu_beta  ~ normal(0, 100);

  sigmasq_y ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001);
  sigmasq_alpha ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001);
  sigmasq_beta ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001);

  alpha ~ normal(mu_alpha, sigma_alpha); // vectorized  
  beta ~ normal(mu_beta, sigma_beta);  // vectorized

  for (nsub in 1:tsub)
    y[nsub] ~ normal( alpha + x[nsub] * beta, sigma_y);
} 

print(fit); shows that parameter estimation was perfect

alpha           6.2e-01  9.8e-04  2.4e-02   5.8e-01   0.62  6.6e-01    594      198  1.0e+00
beta            4.0e+00  1.6e-03  1.9e-02   4.0e+00    4.0  4.0e+00    145       48  1.0e+00

However when I look at the samples for beta parameter (see figure), I notice very long periods of similar values, which then translates into noisy histograms. I cannot come up with an answer, especially because the rats.stan example doesn't behave this way and it is a more complex model.

any ideas would be appreciated.

cheers
s.

messages.author: 70f4b2a8c58d14bd
messages.subject: Re: long autorcorrelations
parts:
I seem to find the source of this behaviour. 

Having adapted the rats.stan to my own data, I have seen now that the rat model is composed of many rats with an hyper-parameter on the top hierarchy. 

In my test, I had only one single group, so the hyper-parameter was actually not informative. 

Removing the hyper-parameter from the model, I managed getting rid of the extremely long auto-correlations.

So my conclusion so far is that too many unnecessary hierarchies might lead to long auto-correlations.

cheers,
s.

messages.author: 146bc26797d1c5e2
messages.subject: Re: long autorcorrelations
parts:
You are right. The model without hierarchy is not identifiable, that is, you can get the same or almost the same likelihood with different parameter combinations. In the model, sigma_y and alpha have identical roles, and beta also has two normal components through mu_beta. The peaky priors for variance may also somehow contribute. The likelihood landscape then becomes difficult for the sampler: either very stretched out on some directions (not corresponding to single parameters), or maybe the curvature varies a lot. 

NUTS requires some care with respect to this kind of issues. 

The stepsize_jitter parameter (see manual) may help if one cannot improve the model.

> On Nov 27, 2014, at 8:06 AM, Janne Sinkkonen <janne.s...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>
> You are right. The model without hierarchy is not identifiable, that is, you can get the same or almost the same likelihood with different parameter combinations. In the model, sigma_y and alpha have identical roles, and beta also has two normal components through mu_beta. The peaky priors for variance may also somehow contribute. The likelihood landscape then becomes difficult for the sampler: either very stretched out on some directions (not corresponding to single parameters), or maybe the curvature varies a lot.
>
> NUTS requires some care with respect to this kind of issues.

So does Gibbs! It's just that Gibbs can move slowly enough that
you don't notice the problem. There's a chapter in the Stan manual
on problematic posteriors that discusses these issues and compares
HMC with Gibbs (and maybe Metropolis --- I can't recall offhand).

I should add some discussion of hierarchical models without
replicates, because then you run into the problems you mention.
> The stepsize_jitter parameter (see manual) may help if one cannot improve the model.

We're more inclined to recommend stepping up target acceptance
rate from 0.8 and stepping down the initial stepsize. Both will
help models avoid getting stuck by making the Hamiltonian simulation
follow the curvature in the posterior more closely. Getting stuck
happens when the step size is too big and the linear approximation
based on the gradient steps too far to accept a proposal --- same as
with too large a step size in Metropolis.

- Bob
